power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

text.text: Background: Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) reduces neonatal mortality and morbidity among preterm and low birthweight (LBW) infants, but implementation and quality vary across sub-Saharan African (SSA) hospitals.

This study reports KMC coverage and quality of care for preterm and LBW neonates admitted to hospitals in the NEST360 Alliance (Kenya, Malawi, Tanzania, Nigeria) and examines the association between KMC provision and survival to discharge.
Methods: NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.
We conducted a cross-sectional study using routinely collected neonatal inpatient data from hospitals participating in the NEST360 Alliance.
Newborns weighing under 2500g were eligible for KMC and included in coverage and quality analyses (January 2021-December 2024).

Quality-of-care cascades quantified attrition along the KMC care pathway from eligibility to successful delivery, defining quality as the proportion of eligible neonates reaching each successive step.

Mixed-effects logistic regression assessed the association between KMC and survival at discharge, including variation by illness severity and, among KMC recipients, by timing of initiation across severity and birthweight strata.
Of 375,238 neonatal admissions across 66 hospitals, 125,844 neonates were eligible for KMC and had KMC documentation available.
Among these, 64,619 (51.3%) received KMC.
All four countries showed improved coverage over the study period, with the largest absolute increases in Nigeria (27.6%) and Tanzania (27.4%).

Excluding Kenya, where KMC timing data were unavailable, 92.1% of neonates started on KMC had a documented start date; of these 44,264 neonates, 12,934 (29.2%) were initiated on KMC on the first day of life.
The quality cascade showed eligible neonates were lost at each step, from eligibility through to documented, timely, and sustained KMC.
Among neonates eligible for both KMC and CPAP, 39.4% of those started on KMC also received documented CPAP at some point during admission.

After adjustment for patient-level factors, receiving KMC was associated with improved survival across all severity groups, with the greatest absolute benefit among the most critically ill neonates (adjusted predicted survival 7% vs 80% without and with KMC, respectively).
KMC coverage improved substantially across NEST360-implementing hospitals between 2021 and 2024, demonstrating progress in implementation.
However, important gaps remain in the quality and timeliness of KMC delivery.

More investment in high-quality KMC implementation, supported by robust monitoring systems linked with quality improvement, are 54 essential to improve outcomes for small and sick newborns across sub-Saharan Africa.

• A quality-of-care cascade, adapted from the HIV clinical cascade, defines quality by progression through successive steps and quantifies losses among eligible neonates at each step towards timely, documented, and sustained KMC, including co-interventions.

• Individually linked records allow each neonate to be followed from admission to discharge or death, enabling adjustment for severity and identification of the specific points at which care is lost, a granularity rarely available in routine aggregated data.

• Of 145,513 KMC-eligible neonates, 125,844 (86.5%) had documentation showing whether KMC was administered or not, and KMC coverage increased across all four countries over the study period, with the largest absolute increases in Nigeria (27.6%) and Tanzania (27.4%).

• However, after excluding Kenyan facilities because KMC timing data were unavailable during the study period, only 7.5% of eligible neonates received KMC on the first day of life, suggesting that timely initiation of KMC remained limited despite WHO guidance recommending immediate initiation.

• Among neonates eligible for both KMC and CPAP, 39.4% of those started on KMC also received documented CPAP administration, highlighting limited delivery of both interventions during admission among neonates with the highest clinical need • After adjustment for patient-level factors, KMC was strongly associated with improved survival across all illness severity groups, with the greatest absolute benefit observed among the most critically ill neonates (adjusted predicted survival 7% vs 80% without and with KMC, respectively).

Newborn Essential Solutions and Technologies (NEST360) is an international alliance of clinical, biomedical, implementation science, and public health experts working with five African governments (Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria, Tanzania, and more recently, Ethiopia) to strengthen level-2 newborn care.

NEST360 supports hospitals through an integrated package of appropriate medical technologies, biomedical engineering, leadership engagement, and strengthened routine health information systems, as well as clinical mentorship, quality improvement coaching, infrastructure support and facilitating exchange visits to high performing sites.
These complementary interventions aim to improve the quality and delivery of evidence-based newborn care, including KMC [21].

text.text: This paper is part of a supplement reporting findings and learnings from the NEST360 Alliance.

We conducted a descriptive analysis of the KMC coverage, quality, and outcomes for LBW neonates across 66 neonatal units in four African countries implementing with NEST360: Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria, and Tanzania.
Data on KMC coverage and quality in routine care in sub-Saharan Africa are limited.
This study addresses this gap using individually linked records and a quality-of-care cascade to identify where neonates are lost along the KMC pathway.
Our objectives were: 1.
KMC Coverage: Describe KMC coverage over time at country population-level for admitted neonates eligible to receive KMC using aggregate data.
KMC quality: Describe quality-of-care cascades including key quality indicators for eligible neonates receiving KMC using individual-level data.

To evaluate the association between KMC and neonatal survival at discharge, and to further assess whether this association varied by illness severity, birthweight, and timing of KMC initiation after accounting for individual-and clustering within hospitals.
This study employed a multi-site, cross-sectional observational design using secondary data analysis.
As part of the NEST360 program, routine data on all neonatal admissions were collected across participating hospitals for the analysis period spanning January 2021 to December 2024.
The study is reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines [22] (see Appendix 1).

text.text: NEST360, established in 2019, has progressively expanded its implementation across 66 newborn units in level 2 hospitals.
The analysis is restricted to hospitals collecting data starting in 2021.
Following implementation, prospective data collection for all newborn admissions has been maintained at participating sites.

The Neonatal Inpatient Dataset (NID) [23] was co-designed with African governments to be a parsimonious individual dataset routinely collected for every newborn admitted to a neonatal ward and used for quality of care improvement on that ward.

text.text: The NID comprises a set of ~55 variables capturing neonatal outcomes, admission details and variables to describe high-impact care.
Trained clerks' abstract information from medical records and input data into REDCap, a secure, web-based platform.
The NID functions as the principal data source in implementing hospitals in Malawi (nationally), Tanzania, and Nigeria.

text.text: To evaluate quality and continuity of care across these domains, three related care cascades were developed.

Kenyan facilities were excluded from all cascade analyses because KMC timing data were unavailable for the study period; breastmilk timing data required for the KMC and nutrition cascade were also unavailable.
For the KMC care cascade, neonates eligible for KMC were defined as all newborns admitted during the study period with birthweight <2500g.

text.text: The cascade assessed, in sequence, documentation of KMC at any point during admission, initiation of KMC, initiation on the day of birth, and continuation of KMC from that first day through to discharge.
Building on this cascade, the KMC and nutrition care cascade evaluated whether neonates initiated on KMC additionally received exclusive breastmilk feeding on the same day through to discharge.
The KMC and CPAP care cascade further assessed integration of respiratory support among neonates eligible for both KMC and CPAP who received KMC and CPAP at any time during admission.
We did not assess whether KMC and CPAP were administered concurrently.

CPAP eligibility was defined as birthweight 1000-1499g, or birthweight 1500-1999g with respiratory distress and hypoxia, in line with clinical criteria applied with NEST360-supported hospitals that is consistent with current evidence [29].

text.text: To evaluate the association between KMC and survival at discharge from the neonatal unit, we conducted both primary and secondary multilevel analyses.
The primary analysis assessed KMC receipt, while the secondary analysis examined the timing of KMC initiation among neonates who received KMC.
Both analyses accounted for baseline illness severity and clustering of neonates within hospitals.

The neonatal severity score was constructed using admission characteristics known to predict neonatal mortality, including gestational age, oxygen saturation at admission, and admission temperature, drawing on established neonatal mortality risk scores developed for lowresource settings [30].
text.formatted: The neonatal severity score was constructed using admission characteristics known to predict neonatal mortality, including gestational age, oxygen saturation at admission, and admission temperature, drawing on established neonatal mortality risk scores developed for lowresource settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Each variable was categorized into clinically meaningful severity strata and assigned ordinal scores reflecting increasing physiological instability.
Individual component scores were summed to generate a composite severity score, which was subsequently categorized into mild (3-4), moderate (5-6), and severe (7-9) illness groups (Appendix 7).
The scoring framework was developed and piloted using neonatal inpatient data to assess its ability to predict survival at discharge.
In the previously published CPAP analysis [40], the mixed-effects survival model incorporating clinical severity demonstrated good discrimination (AUC = 0.74).
text.formatted: In the previously published CPAP analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[40]</ref>, the mixed-effects survival model incorporating clinical severity demonstrated good discrimination (AUC = 0.74).

text.text: The severity score was subsequently applied in the present study to account for baseline illness severity when examining the association between KMC receipt and survival at discharge.
The association between KMC receipt and survival at discharge was assessed using mixedeffects logistic regression, with survival modeled as a binary outcome.
The model included KMC coverage (receiving any KMC), baseline illness severity, sex, and birth location as fixed effects, with facility included as a random intercept to account for clustering.
An interaction between KMC receipt and illness severity was included to assess whether the association with survival varied by baseline severity.
The contribution of the interaction was evaluated using a likelihood ratio test comparing models with and without the interaction term.
Adjusted predicted probabilities of survival and corresponding 95% confidence intervals were estimated across severity categories using marginal effects.
Among neonates who received KMC, a secondary mixed-effects logistic regression analysis assessed the association between timing of KMC initiation and survival at discharge.
Kenya was excluded from this analysis because KMC initiation timing was not routinely collected.
Neonates from other countries with missing or undocumented KMC initiation timing were also excluded.

Among eligible KMC recipients with documented initiation timing, timing of KMC initiation was categorized as same-day initiation (≤24 hours), early initiation (1-3 days), delayed initiation (3-7 days), and late initiation (>7 days).
text.formatted: Among eligible KMC recipients with documented initiation timing, timing of KMC initiation was categorized as same-day initiation (≤24 hours), early initiation (1-3 days), delayed initiation (3-7 days), and late initiation (>7 days).

text.text: The model additionally adjusted for illness severity category, birthweight category, sex, and birth location, with hospital included as a random intercept.
All analyses were conducted in R version 4.2.2.
Mixed-effects logistic regression models were fitted using the lme4 package, with hospital included as a random intercept to account for clustering of neonates within hospitals.
Adjusted predicted probabilities and marginal effects were estimated using the emmeans package in R. Model discrimination was assessed using ROC curves and AUC statistics.
Statistical significance was evaluated using two-sided tests with an alpha level of 0.05.
Between 1 January 2021 and 31 December 2024, 375,238 newborns were admitted across 66 neonatal units in the four countries (Malawi = 37, Kenya = 13, Nigeria = 9, Tanzania = 7).
Malawi is the only country-wide scale which accounts for the disproportionate number of sites in this country.

Of these newborns, 145,513 met criteria for KMC eligibility, of whom 125,844 (86.5%) had KMC documentation (administered or not administered), as shown in Figure 1 (Malawi: n = 68,274; Kenya: n = 37,282; Tanzania: n = 17,613; Nigeria: n = 2,675).

text.text: Objective 2: Quality 108,221 neonates were eligible for inclusion in the quality analysis.
text.formatted: <head>Objective 2: Quality</head> 108,221 neonates were eligible for inclusion in the quality analysis.

text.text: 88,562 (81.8%) had documentation indicating whether KMC was administered, of whom 48,047 (54.3%) were started on KMC.
Among those started on KMC, 44,264 (92.1%) had a valid start date recorded, indicating a relatively small gap in start-date documentation.
Of newborns with a start date, only 12,934 neonates (29.2%) were documented as having KMC initiated on the day of birth.
Of these, 8,110 (62.7%) neonates were documented as receiving KMC through to discharge.
Across the entire cascade, only 8,110 (7.5%) of 108,221 KMC-eligible neonates were both initiated on KMC on the first day of life and retained in KMC care until discharge (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Across the entire cascade, only 8,110 (7.5%) of 108,221 KMC-eligible neonates were both initiated on KMC on the first day of life and retained in KMC care until discharge (Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>).

text.text: Among the 44,264 neonates who had a documented KMC start date, 30,003 (67.8%) received breastmilk within the first day of life.
Of those who initiated breastmilk early, 29,448 (98.2%) were exclusively breastfed at discharge.

However, because only 44,264 of 108,221 eligible neonates were started on KMC with a documented start date, largely because nearly half of neonates with documented KMC status were not started on KMC, the proportion of all KMC-eligible neonates who both received KMC and were documented as having initiated early breastmilk feeding was substantially lower (Figure 4).

text.text: Overall, 29,448 (27.2%) of KMC-eligible neonates were initiated on KMC and received breastmilk on the same day, with both interventions continued through to discharge.
Kenyan facilities were excluded from this cascade because KMC timing data were unavailable during the study period.

Among the 25,654 neonates eligible for both KMC and CPAP, 22,241 (86.7%) had a documented record of whether or not they received KMC, of whom 11,985 (53.9%) were started on KMC and had start date documented.

Of those, only 4,720 (39.4%) also received CPAP during admission, demonstrating that concurrent delivery of KMC and respiratory support was achieved in only a small minority of neonates who required both interventions (Figure 5).

text.text: Overall, only 4,720 (18.4%) of the 25,654 KMC-and CPAP-eligible neonates had documented receipt of both KMC and CPAP during admission.

After adjusting for patient-level characteristics, and clustering within hospitals, neonates documented as receiving KMC consistently demonstrated markedly higher predicted probabilities of survival across all severity categories.

Both the absolute and relative survival advantages associated with KMC increased progressively with worsening clinical severity, with the greatest differences observed among severely ill neonates (Table 1).
text.formatted: Both the absolute and relative survival advantages associated with KMC increased progressively with worsening clinical severity, with the greatest differences observed among severely ill neonates (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Overall, after adjustment for patient-level characteristics, and hospital-level clustering, KMC receipt was associated with higher survival across all illness severity groups (Tables 1 and 2).
text.formatted: Overall, after adjustment for patient-level characteristics, and hospital-level clustering, KMC receipt was associated with higher survival across all illness severity groups (Tables <ref type="table">1</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref>).

text.text: The association between KMC and survival varied significantly by baseline illness severity, with the magnitude of the association increasing with greater severity.

Among neonates with mild illness, KMC was associated with substantially higher odds of survival (aOR 10.39, 95% CI 9.67-11.16), with significant interaction effects observed for moderate (interaction aOR 2.29, 95% CI 2.06-2.55) and severe illness (interaction aOR 4.99, 95% CI 3.91-6.35).
Increasing illness severity was independently associated with lower odds of survival.
Male and outborn neonates also had lower adjusted odds of survival than female and inborn neonates, respectively (Table 2).

text.text: Figure 6 presents the adjusted predicted probability of survival across neonatal severity groups for babies who received KMC versus those who did not receive KMC, after adjustment for illness severity, their interaction, sex, and birth location, with hospital included as a random intercept.

text.text: Adjusted predicted probabilities from the mixed-effects logistic regression model demonstrated progressively lower survival with increasing clinical severity among neonates who did not receive KMC.
In contrast, neonates receiving KMC maintained substantially higher predicted survival across all severity groups.

The magnitude of the difference between KMC and non-KMC groups increased with severity, with the largest separation observed among severely ill neonates, supporting a significant interaction between KMC and severity category.
The gap between the KMC and non-KMC groups widens as severity increases.
The association between KMC and survival becomes stronger with increasing neonatal severity.

The mixed-effects KMC survival model demonstrated good discrimination, with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.8699, indicating that the model has an 87% probability of correctly distinguishing between a neonate who survived and one who did not survive (Appendix 3).

Among neonates who received KMC, later KMC initiation was associated with higher adjusted survival compared with same-day initiation after accounting for baseline illness severity, birthweight, sex, birth location, and facility-level clustering.

Adjusted predicted probabilities showed lower survival with increasing baseline illness severity across KMC initiation groups, with the lowest predicted survival observed among severely ill neonates receiving same-day KMC (Figure 7).
text.formatted: Adjusted predicted probabilities showed lower survival with increasing baseline illness severity across KMC initiation groups, with the lowest predicted survival observed among severely ill neonates receiving same-day KMC (Figure <ref type="figure">7</ref>).

text.text: However, the apparent survival advantage associated with later initiation should be interpreted cautiously, as neonates in the delayed and late initiation groups had necessarily survived long enough to receive KMC, introducing potential survivor selection bias.
Detailed adjusted estimates are presented in Appendix 4.
In these analyses, later KMC initiation remained positively associated with survival, while greater illness severity, male sex, and outborn status were associated with lower survival.
Birthweight was also strongly associated with survival, with progressively higher adjusted odds among higher birthweight categories (Appendix 4).
Birthweight-stratified predicted probabilities further showed that differences in survival by timing of KMC initiation were most pronounced among smaller and more severely ill neonates (Appendix 4).
These secondary findings should therefore be interpreted as associations rather than evidence that delaying KMC improves survival.
To support the use of these findings in clinical training and advocacy, a plain-language summary of the key associations has been developed and is presented in Appendix 5.

This study presents a large multi-country analysis of KMC coverage and quality in sub-Saharan Africa, drawing on prospectively collected, individually-linked data from 66 hospitals across four countries over a four-year period.

By adapting quality-of-care cascades such as used from HIV, to KMC and to other neonatal care interventions [31] [32] [33] , this analysis quantifies where, and to what extent, eligible neonates are lost from the care pathway.
text.formatted: By adapting quality-of-care cascades such as used from HIV, to KMC and to other neonatal care interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[33]</ref> , this analysis quantifies where, and to what extent, eligible neonates are lost from the care pathway.

text.text: These results challenge the tendency to treat KMC coverage as a unitary indicator and demonstrates the analytical value of disaggregating the care pathway to identify where, and for whom, delivery of evidence-based KMC care consistently falls short.

Across these 65 sites in the four countries, KMC coverage increased over the study period, with Nigeria and Tanzania recording the largest absolute increases (27.6 and 27.4 percentage points, respectively).

Malawi's higher baseline coverage, with steady and sustained improvement in coverage builds on long-standing national institutionalisation of KMC, having integrated the intervention into national guidelines as early as 2005, and pre-service training established.

This extended implementation history may have fostered greater acceptability among both healthcare staff and caregivers, and created conditions in which localised adaptations, such as hospital-level innovations in KMC positioning support, could be established and sustained [34] [35] [36].
text.formatted: This extended implementation history may have fostered greater acceptability among both healthcare staff and caregivers, and created conditions in which localised adaptations, such as hospital-level innovations in KMC positioning support, could be established and sustained <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[34]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[35]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[36]</ref>.

text.text: Nigeria's coverage figures may reflect national newborn care policies and the establishment of KMC champions at hospital level [37, 38].
text.formatted: Nigeria's coverage figures may reflect national newborn care policies and the establishment of KMC champions at hospital level <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">38]</ref>.

text.text: Tanzania's improvements in overall coverage, alongside coverage in the 2000-2499g category that, despite marked improvement, remained below that of other weight categories, illustrate a pattern observed across settings in which policy revision precedes changes in clinical practice, as the 2022 extension of KMC eligibility to all infants under 2500g does not appear to have been fully operationalised in this weight category within the study period.

In Kenya, coverage increased gradually but at a slower pace than other countries, reflecting documented challenges in translating national policy into consistent frontline practice, including resource constraints, limited staff time, which have been identified as barriers to sustained uptake [39].
text.formatted: In Kenya, coverage increased gradually but at a slower pace than other countries, reflecting documented challenges in translating national policy into consistent frontline practice, including resource constraints, limited staff time, which have been identified as barriers to sustained uptake <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[39]</ref>.

text.text: Infrastructural limitations have also been identified as barrier to high quality KMC in Kenya [40].
text.formatted: Infrastructural limitations have also been identified as barrier to high quality KMC in Kenya <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[40]</ref>.

text.text: Notably, Kenya's expansion of free maternity services has increased demand for hospital-based newborn care, and it is plausible that growth in the volume of eligible neonates outpaced the expansion of KMC capacity, contributing to lower overall coverage rates [41].
text.formatted: Notably, Kenya's expansion of free maternity services has increased demand for hospital-based newborn care, and it is plausible that growth in the volume of eligible neonates outpaced the expansion of KMC capacity, contributing to lower overall coverage rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[41]</ref>.

text.text: It is important to note that these findings are drawn entirely from NEST data collection, which operated at scale only in Malawi; coverage trends for Kenya, Nigeria, and Tanzania therefore may not be representative of national-level trends in those countries.

Taken together, these country-level findings underscore that coverage trajectories are shaped by the intersection of policy maturity, health system capacity, and equity, and that strategies to improve KMC uptake must be context-specific.
The quality cascade findings carry direct implications for how KMC programmes in LMICs are designed, monitored, and resourced.

The most striking observation is the marked gap in the timeliness of initiation: only around one in eight eligible neonates (12.0%) were recorded to be initiated on KMC on the first day of life, and fewer than one in ten (7.5%) were initiated on the first day and continued through to discharge, despite guidance explicitly recommending initiation as soon as possible after birth [11].

text.text: The finding that most KMC in this cohort was not initiated on the first day of life may not be due to clinical prioritisation, but the practical consequences of an infrastructure gap.

The 2022 WHO policy recommending KMC prior to clinical stability was published only shortly before the latter years of this study's analysis period, and evidence from comparable level-2 care settings in sub-Saharan Africa suggests that substantial hospital-level infrastructure improvements are required to implement KMC prior to stability safely [8, 42].

text.text: Where the conditions for safe early initiation do not yet exist, premature implementation carries clinical risk, and programmes must therefore ensure that advocacy for earlier KMC is accompanied by proportionate investment in the enabling and necessary infrastructure.

Programmes should also consider incorporating timeliness of initiation as a standard quality indicator alongside coverage, shifting monitoring frameworks towards the concept of effective coverage, which accounts for both coverage and the quality of the care delivered.
Infrastructure and workforce readiness are critical determinants of whether KMC can be delivered consistently at the hospital level.
Service readiness assessments across these same hospitals and time periods have highlighted substantial gaps in the infrastructure needed to support small and sick newborn care [31].

text.text: Bed occupancy was highly variable, with almost a third of hospital-months exceeding full capacity, and nursing staffing ratios, particularly at night, frequently fell short of recommended levels, especially in Kenya [31].

text.text: Family-centred care, which encompasses KMC, parental involvement, and the support systems needed to sustain these practices, was the most poorly resourced component of neonatal care across all four countries at just 27% [IQR 18-40%] [19].

text.text: These gaps extended beyond equipment to the workforce capacity and physical environment needed to support mothers and families in practising KMC, highlighting that hospital readiness for KMC remains substantially limited across these settings.

Translating policy into consistent practice requires a paradigm shift towards care of the mother-infant dyad, supported by a whole-systems approach addressing workforce, infrastructure, and institutional culture.
The co-intervention cascades provide additional insight into the co-coverage of newborn care interventions.
Within the nutrition cascade, 67.8% of neonates with a documented KMC start date received breastmilk on the first day of life, and of those, 98.2% were exclusively breastfed at discharge.
While these figures are encouraging, they must be interpreted in the context of the substantially reduced denominator at this stage of the cascade.

The apparent success in breastfeeding applies only to those neonates who had already progressed through earlier documentation and initiation steps, and therefore could reflect a selected group receiving more consistent overall care.
Early initiation of breastfeeding within the first hour of life is associated with sustained exclusive breastfeeding and reduced neonatal mortality [44, 45].
text.formatted: Early initiation of breastfeeding within the first hour of life is associated with sustained exclusive breastfeeding and reduced neonatal mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[44,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">45]</ref>.

text.text: However, NEST360 currently records breastmilk initiation only by day of life, meaning that this one-hour target cannot be assessed.
Capturing timing of first feed in hours would enable hospitals to determine whether practice aligns with this recommendation and to identify modifiable delays in early initiation.
Within the CPAP cascade, among neonates receiving KMC who were also assessed as requiring CPAP, about 39.4% had CPAP administered.
As with the primary cascade, it is not possible to determine whether this reflects under-delivery of respiratory support, incomplete documentation, or both.

However, given that a significant proportion of KMC-eligible neonates will also require concurrent respiratory support, this figure warrants attention and reinforces the case for strengthening both clinical capacity and documentation systems for co-interventions alongside KMC.

The greatest loss along the cascade occurred at KMC initiation, where 45.7% of neonates with documented KMC status were not started on KMC, considerably larger than the loss attributable to documentation gaps (18.2%).
This indicates that non-provision of KMC, rather than failure to record it, is the major driver of the coverage shortfall observed.

Nonetheless, documentation gaps remain a systemic challenge in routine data capture rather than a problem specific to any single intervention, and routine data cannot fully distinguish nondelivery of care from failure to document care that was provided.
Evidence from comparable settings indicates that the absence of standardised recording tools and reporting processes is a recognised barrier to monitoring progress at scale [46, 47].
text.formatted: Evidence from comparable settings indicates that the absence of standardised recording tools and reporting processes is a recognised barrier to monitoring progress at scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[46,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">47]</ref>.

text.text: Strengthening and standardising documentation of KMC must therefore be treated as an integral component of programme design and scale up [48] [49] [50], both to improve the accuracy of coverage estimates and to ensure that monitoring frameworks can meaningfully distinguish between failure to deliver and failure to record.

text.text: Survival outcomes were analysed across birthweight and severity strata.

These findings suggest that the observed relationship between KMC timing and survival is strongly influenced by baseline neonatal risk, with timing becoming less prognostically important among larger neonates who generally experienced favourable survival outcomes across all timing groups.

These findings also suggest that although increasing illness severity markedly reduced neonatal survival, KMC remained strongly associated with improved survival and appeared to provide the greatest relative benefit among the most critically ill neonates.
The findings of this study must also be considered in light of recent evidence on the benefits of KMC prior to stability.
Recent evidence indicates that immediate KMC for infants weighing 1.0 to 1.799kg, regardless of clinical stability, may reduce neonatal mortality by up to 25% [28].
text.formatted: Recent evidence indicates that immediate KMC for infants weighing 1.0 to 1.799kg, regardless of clinical stability, may reduce neonatal mortality by up to 25% <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[28]</ref>.

text.text: While KMC prior to stabilisation does not significantly affect early neonatal mortality at fewer than seven days, likley since these very vulnerable babies need more intensive care, it has been shown to reduce in 28-day mortality in both iKMC trial and OMWANA, especially with higher duration [8].
text.formatted: While KMC prior to stabilisation does not significantly affect early neonatal mortality at fewer than seven days, likley since these very vulnerable babies need more intensive care, it has been shown to reduce in 28-day mortality in both iKMC trial and OMWANA, especially with higher duration <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[8]</ref>.

text.text: These findings strengthen the case for earlier initiation and higher duration each day during admission and after lend urgency to the infrastructure investments discussed above.

The fact that fewer than one in ten eligible neonates in this cohort received KMC on the first day of life must therefore be understood not only as a quality gap, but as a missed opportunity to deliver an intervention with meaningful survival benefit.
Our analysis has a number of methodological strengths.
The scale and longitudinal nature of the dataset, encompassing over 145,000 KMC-eligible neonates across 66 hospitals and four years, provides statistical power and cross-country comparability.

Unlike aggregated national estimates, individually linked inpatient data from the NID allow each neonate to be followed from admission to discharge or death, enabling multi-stage quality cascades, adjustment for severity, and identification of the specific points at which care is lost.
This granularity represents the principal contribution of the NID to understanding, and improving, the delivery of small and sick newborn care.

The development of coverage indicators for KMC within routine health information systems remains an active area of international policy work, with individual case-note data recognised as the most appropriate source for capturing inpatient KMC indicators, despite known data quality challenges [46].
text.formatted: The development of coverage indicators for KMC within routine health information systems remains an active area of international policy work, with individual case-note data recognised as the most appropriate source for capturing inpatient KMC indicators, despite known data quality challenges <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[46]</ref>.

text.text: This study demonstrates that structured improvement programmes can achieve meaningful and sustained increases in KMC coverage across diverse health system contexts in sub-Saharan Africa.
However, the cascade analyses presented here reveal that coverage, as conventionally measured, is an insufficient indicator of programmatic success.

The stepwise losses from eligibility to documented, timely, and continuous KMC delivery illustrate that the distance between a policy commitment to KMC and its realisation as effective care remains considerable.
The 2023 WHO Global Position Paper on KMC calls for a fundamental reorganisation of maternal-newborn care, with immediate initiation following birth as the new standard of practice [51].
text.formatted: The 2023 WHO Global Position Paper on KMC calls for a fundamental reorganisation of maternal-newborn care, with immediate initiation following birth as the new standard of practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[51]</ref>.

text.text: Achieving this standard across high-burden settings will require investment not only in clinical training and commodities, but in the data systems, institutional accountability structures, and enabling environments that include infrastructural changes to support the mother-infant dyad.
Several limitations must be acknowledged.
Firstly, there was a substantial amount of missing data for KMC and birthweight.

It is plausible that the most critically ill and smallest neonates were least likely to have accurately recorded birthweight and KMC data, which would mean these neonates are under-represented in the analysed sample and could bias the birthweightand severity-stratified findings.
KMC timing data were unavailable for Kenyan facilities, which were therefore excluded from all cascade analyses.

Elsewhere, start dates were documented for 92.1% of neonates started on KMC, so missing timing data are unlikely to have substantially affected estimates of timely initiation, although the proportion initiated on the first day of life (12.0%) should be considered as underestimated.
Data completeness in routine hospital records across LMICs is highly heterogeneous, and incomplete recording in nonstandardised case notes may systematically underrepresent indicator values [52].
text.formatted: Data completeness in routine hospital records across LMICs is highly heterogeneous, and incomplete recording in nonstandardised case notes may systematically underrepresent indicator values <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[52]</ref>.

text.text: These limitations highlight gaps in the infrastructure that support consistent care delivery.

The analysis is further limited to NEST360 phase 1 implementation hospitals, which received structured programme support to support KMC uptake and are therefore unlikely to be representative of the broader hospital landscape in each country.
Findings should be interpreted in this context and not generalised to non-programme settings without caution.
A limitation is the absence of a KMC duration indicator generally and also within NEST360 data systems.
Duration of skin-to-skin contact per day is a major determinant of KMC health impact [53, 54], which reflects a current gap in NEST360 data collection.
text.formatted: Duration of skin-to-skin contact per day is a major determinant of KMC health impact <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[53,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">54]</ref>, which reflects a current gap in NEST360 data collection.

For the world's smallest and most vulnerable newborns, the gap between what is known to work and what is delivered results in lives lost.

Closing that gap demands a shift from measuring whether KMC is offered to ensuring coverage and quality are tracked and data used for KMC for every eligible newborn at the right time and duration in every hospital, and country.

As national targets to ending preventable neonatal deaths approach their 2030 deadline, the evidence presented here underscores that scale-up of small and sick newborn care must be accompanied by sustained investment in quality, accountability, and the health systems capable of delivering both.
For the world's smallest and most vulnerable newborns, the gap between what is known to work and what is consistently delivered represents a preventable loss of life.
Closing that gap demands a shift from measuring whether KMC is offered to ensuring it is delivered equitably, safely, and at the right time, for every eligible newborn in every country.
